summary:
AstroSentry is an interactive web application that brings NASA's SPHEREx mission to everyone, making it possible to explore the infrared sky and investigate how it changes over time. Our platform transforms real astronomical observations into an accessible visual experience.

Users can navigate an interactive sky map, explore 100 infrared spectral channels, and compare 23 real observations across six prepared astronomical fields. Temporal playback, blink comparison, and image differencing help reveal changes that may be difficult to notice in individual observations.

AstroSentry also provides scientific tools for examining potential moving objects, understanding measurement uncertainties, and documenting candidate investigations. Our scientific backend demonstrates coordinate-based observation retrieval, FITS processing, and dynamic temporal sequence generation in a locally validated prototype.

By reducing technical barriers to astronomical data exploration, AstroSentry empowers students, amateur astronomers, researchers, and curious minds to investigate high-proper-motion stars, brown dwarfs, variable stars, and potential undiscovered objects in our Solar System.

Our mission is simple: Beyond what the eye can see.
details:
What exactly does it do?

AstroSentry is an interactive astronomical exploration platform designed to make NASA's SPHEREx observations accessible to everyone. It addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by helping users visualize how the sky changes over time and investigate potential moving objects through real scientific observations.

Our application provides:

  • Interactive all-sky exploration: Navigate the infrared sky using real SPHEREx imagery and explore 100 selectable spectral channels to discover how astronomical structures appear at different wavelengths.
  • Coordinate-based investigations: Our locally validated scientific backend supports Right Ascension and Declination queries, retrieval of available SPHEREx observations, and dynamic preparation of temporal image sequences.
  • Temporal visualization: Play observations taken at different dates, switch between epochs, and use Blink to compare images while maintaining a fixed camera position.
  • Scientific analysis: Inspect observation dates, wavelengths, detector information, apparent motion, measurement uncertainties, and image differences where suitable data are available.
  • Candidate Explorer: Mark potential moving objects, document observations, and save or export candidate investigations for further review.
  • Guided Discovery: Explore prepared astronomical fields and learn how real observations can be interpreted responsibly.

The public application includes six prepared fields: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis, and the Pinwheel Galaxy (M101), with 23 real observations available for temporal exploration.

These fields include all five astronomical targets highlighted in the challenge, allowing visitors to investigate different scientific phenomena without requiring specialized software, programming knowledge, or access to our backend.

How does it work?

AstroSentry combines an interactive web application with a modular scientific processing pipeline.

The public application provides all-sky exploration, spectral visualization, and prepared temporal sequences. The complete coordinate-based scientific workflow has also been implemented and demonstrated locally, although live generation of new sequences is not enabled in the current public deployment.

Our scientific workflow consists of six steps:

  1. Sky exploration: The user navigates an interactive celestial map based on the official SPHEREx DR1 all-sky spectral cube. Different wavelengths reveal different structures in the infrared sky.
  2. Coordinate selection: In the dynamic workflow, the user identifies a region by entering celestial coordinates, choosing a field width, and selecting a detector.
  3. Observation retrieval: Our Python backend queries NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) using the official SIA2 protocol to identify available SPHEREx observations. Relevant scientific images are retrieved as FITS files through the archive's Cutout Service.
  4. Scientific processing: The pipeline uses World Coordinate System (WCS) information to align observations to a common celestial grid. It handles invalid pixels and quality masks, preserves observation metadata, and applies consistent visualization settings to prepare comparable image sequences.
  5. Temporal investigation: Observations are displayed chronologically. Users can play the sequence, compare selected epochs with Blink, inspect scientific metadata, and examine image differences where suitable data are available.
  6. Evidence documentation: Users can identify interesting features, record potential candidates, and export their findings for further investigation.

This workflow transforms complex scientific data into an accessible visual experience while preserving the provenance and scientific meaning of the original observations.

What makes our project creative?

AstroSentry combines the experience of exploring an interactive sky map with the capabilities of a scientific time-domain investigation tool.

Instead of requiring users to manually download FITS files, understand complex astronomical formats, or write their own processing scripts, our platform brings these operations together in an intuitive visual workflow.

Our key innovation is connecting three complementary perspectives:

  • Space: Where is the object in the sky?
  • Wavelength: How does its appearance change across the infrared spectrum?
  • Time: How does it change between observations?

By combining these perspectives, AstroSentry helps users investigate potentially interesting astronomical changes while considering differences caused by wavelength, image quality, or instrumental effects.

The application goes beyond visualization by providing temporal playback, image comparison, scientific inspection, and candidate documentation within the same environment.

Our Guided Discovery experience introduces users to real astronomical objects, while Candidate Explorer encourages them to move from passive observation to active investigation.

AstroSentry makes the process of exploring scientific data feel intuitive, interactive, and engaging while encouraging responsible scientific interpretation.

What benefits does it have?

Scientific: AstroSentry makes it easier to examine temporal changes, compare astronomical observations, and identify potential candidates for more detailed investigation. Scientific metadata and measurement uncertainties help users distinguish interesting observations from confirmed results.

Educational: Students and educators can explore real space mission data and learn about infrared astronomy, celestial coordinates, stellar motion, brown dwarfs, variable stars, and astronomical image processing through interactive examples.

Social: The application reduces barriers to participation in astronomy by providing an accessible public web interface that does not require specialized scientific software or advanced programming knowledge. It encourages curiosity and makes real astronomical investigation more approachable.

Technological: Our modular scientific pipeline separates data acquisition, image processing, visualization, and candidate documentation. This structure allows the platform to evolve as new SPHEREx observations become available and provides a foundation for expanding its scientific capabilities.

What do we hope to achieve?

Our short-term goal is to make SPHEREx data easier to explore and demonstrate how real observations can reveal changes in the sky.

By combining spectral exploration with temporal visualization, we hope to help people understand that the universe is not static and that comparing observations over time can provide valuable scientific insights.

In the long term, we hope to support a broader citizen-science community in which anyone can investigate astronomical phenomena, document potential moving objects, and contribute useful observations for professional review.

Future development will focus on expanding the number of prepared fields, enabling public coordinate-based sequence generation, improving automated candidate identification, and strengthening scientific validation.

AstroSentry is inspired by the search for undiscovered objects in our Solar System, including the hypothetical Planet X. However, we do not claim to have discovered a new planet or confirmed a previously unknown moving object.

Our aim is to provide the tools that make such investigations more accessible, helping transform curiosity into meaningful scientific exploration.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

Frontend and visualization

  • React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML and CSS.
  • Aladin Lite for interactive astronomical sky visualization and georeferenced image layers.
  • HiPS and WCS for celestial image visualization and coordinate alignment.

Backend and scientific processing

  • Python.
  • NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, Astroquery, Reproject, Matplotlib and Pillow.
  • FITS scientific image processing, coordinate transformations, quality masks, centroid estimation, image alignment, and temporal comparison.
  • NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA2 and Cutout Service for access to SPHEREx observations.

Astronomical data and resources

  • SPHEREx Data Release 1 (DR1) spectral images and all-sky spectral cube.
  • SPHEREx Quick Release 3 (QR3) spectral images.
  • Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS) imagery for complementary historical sky exploration.
  • SIMBAD astronomical database for object identification and reference information.

Infrastructure and deployment

  • Git and GitHub for version control.
  • Vercel for public frontend hosting.
  • Raspberry Pi 5 with 8 GB RAM, Debian Linux, Waitress, SQLite and systemd for the scientific backend.
  • Tailscale for secure connectivity during backend testing.

Development and validation

  • Visual Studio Code, npm, pytest, Ruff and Playwright.
  • OpenAI ChatGPT and Codex for AI-assisted planning, software architecture, development, debugging, testing, and documentation.
  • Real astronomical data and reproducible scientific validation procedures.

Scientific validation and current status

AstroSentry's public application is deployed at https://astrosentry.vercel.app and provides interactive all-sky exploration, 100 selectable spectral channels, and temporal visualization of 23 real observations across six prepared astronomical fields.

These include all five official challenge targets:

  • Barnard's Star: 2 observations.
  • Epsilon Indi B: 6 observations.
  • WISE 0855: 5 observations.
  • RW Aurigae: 3 observations.
  • R Draconis: 5 observations.

The additional Pinwheel Galaxy (M101) field contains 2 observations.

The public application supports temporal playback, Blink comparison, observation metadata, scientific inspection, and candidate documentation. Image differencing is available for suitable prepared observations.

We have also implemented and demonstrated a scientific backend for coordinate-based observation retrieval, FITS processing, WCS alignment, and dynamic temporal sequence generation. This pipeline has been validated locally using real SPHEREx observations.

A protected Raspberry Pi deployment has passed installation, scientific import, health endpoint, HTTPS connectivity, and service restart checks. Anonymous cached access and archive error resilience have also been implemented and tested locally.

For this submission, the dynamic backend remains private. Public visitors can explore the prepared sequences without requiring an account or access code, but cannot request live acquisition and processing of new observations for arbitrary coordinates.

Our final frontend has been validated on desktop and mobile, including successful playback of all six prepared fields with the backend unavailable. Scientific data integrity has also been verified through reproducible hash checks.

Our investigation of Epsilon Indi B produced an exploratory apparent displacement measurement. This result is not presented as a statistically confirmed detection. Other fields illustrate the importance of image quality, wavelength compatibility, and measurement uncertainty.

AstroSentry uses authentic astronomical observations, preserves data provenance, and distinguishes measured results from potential candidates. We do not claim to have discovered Planet X or any previously unknown astronomical object.

Our vision

The universe contains extraordinary information that is invisible to the human eye. SPHEREx gives us the opportunity to explore that information through infrared observations, and AstroSentry aims to make that exploration available to everyone.

We believe that scientific curiosity should not be limited by technical expertise. By bringing space, wavelength, and time together, AstroSentry opens a new way to experience the sky and investigate its hidden changes.

AstroSentry — Beyond what the eye can see.
